title: Views of self (section 31)
hook: views of self and being are not views; so they are called views

segments.voice: Yesterday, dust and worlds: a world ground to specks, and neither world nor dust a fixed thing. Your line: a world of dust.

Two friends walk out of a movie. One says, that was brilliant. The other says, that was a mess. By the parking lot, it's no longer about the movie. Each is defending something closer to home: my taste, my judgment, me. A view started as a way of seeing a film and became a wall to stand behind. Section thirty-one of the Diamond Sutra goes after the view under all the others, the view of a self. And it doesn't swap it for a better view. It does something quieter.
screen: `BRILLIANT. A MESS.` → `NOT ABOUT THE MOVIE NOW.` → `THE VIEW UNDER THE VIEWS.`

segments.voice: The Buddha asks Subhuti, in paraphrase: if someone said the Tathagata taught a view of a self, a being, a living soul, a person, would they be speaking rightly? No, says Subhuti. What the Tathagata taught as a view of self is taught as no view, and that is why it's called a view of self. The same four ideas the sutra has cut since its opening sections come back one last time, and this time it isn't the self being cut. It's the view of it. Then the Buddha says that one who sets out on this path should know all things, see all things, and trust all things in such a way that they don't hold on to even an idea of a thing. And of course: an idea of a thing is no idea; that's why it's called an idea. Even the sutra's own teaching about no self is not a new belief to clutch. Look back at the week. No beings freed: help without the ledger. Form and sound: not the face or the voice. Not annihilation, and still not nothing. Merit not held. Neither coming nor going. Dust and worlds. Now views of self. Every day the blade had the same edge. It doesn't throw away beings, bodies, merit or worlds. It takes away the grip. Today it reaches a deeper one: the grip on being right about who we are.
screen: `DID HE TEACH A VIEW OF SELF?` · `NO VIEW, SO CALLED A VIEW.` · `NOT EVEN AN IDEA OF A THING.` · `THE WEEK: THE GRIP, NOT THE THING.` · then, large: `SO-CALLED VIEWS.`

segments.voice: Pick up one opinion you hold firmly, about a person, a habit, a team, or yourself, and let it sit in your mind like a stone in an open palm. Notice where it presses: the jaw, the chest, the hands. Don't drop it and don't argue with it; just loosen the fingers, and let the breath move around it.
Views of self. Section thirty-one: what the Tathagata taught as a view of self is taught as no view, and so it's called a view. Today's word.
Your line: so-called views. A view held in an open palm, not a fist. That's day one thousand one hundred forty-eight, and that's the week.

howItsDone: Mahayana teachers read section 31 of the Diamond Sutra as a warning not to turn the teaching of no self into one more view to defend; students meet it in chanting, study and meditation on how views are held.

original.note: Sanskrit (Pali ditthi): a view, a way of seeing; in section 31, the 'view of self' that is no view.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism replaces 'I have a self' with 'I have no self.'
what it means: the sutra won't let either become a view to clutch; even the idea of a thing is 'so called.'
what a scholar hears: section 31 moves from the four ideas of self, being, soul and person to the views of them, and ends on not holding even an idea of a dharma.

chat.says: If the sutra cuts the self, isn't 'no self' just the new belief to hold on to?
options: The sutra says even an idea of a thing is no idea, so even 'no self' isn't to be clutched.
The sutra stops at the self; ideas and views are left for each person to keep.
No self only applies to monks, so lay people can keep their view of self.
chat.meaning: Section thirty-one cuts the grip on views too: a view of self is taught as no view, and even an idea of a thing isn't held.

Tathagata.meaning: the awakened one; a title the Buddha uses for himself

Subhuti.meaning: the elder who questions the Buddha in the Diamond Sutra

Diamond Sutra.meaning: a short Mahayana sutra that cuts through every grip
